HORN LAKE – The DeSoto County District Attorney’s Office is seeking no bond for a Horn Lake man accused in a shooting earlier this week at Discount Market on Goodman Road.

District Attorney Matthew Barton announced that his office has filed a petition asking the court to deny bond for 22-year-old Taderius Young of Horn Lake following the shooting.

Young was taken into custody and charged with aggravated assault in connection with the incident. He is being held at the DeSoto County Adult Detention Center.

In addition to the aggravated assault charge, prosecutors said Young has also been charged with auto burglary in a separate case. The district attorney’s office said that charge stemmed from a case previously secured through a secret indictment in February.

According to the filing, the state argues that Young poses a special danger to the community under Article 3, Section 29 of the Mississippi Constitution and should be held without bond.

“Young has made it abundantly clear that our community isn’t safe without him in custody,” Barton said. “That is why we are asking the court to deny his bond and keep him exactly where he belongs, behind bars.”

Barton said his office plans to pursue every legal avenue available to hold violent offenders accountable.

“Let this be a message to violent criminals,” Barton said. “We don’t play here. If you bring violence into our community, we will find you, we will charge you, and, as Young is about to find out, we are going to aggressively prosecute you.”

The case was investigated by the Horn Lake Police Department.

TUPELO — The Natchez Trace Parkway will close the Double Arch Bridge near Nashville beginning April 15 for construction of a permanent pedestrian safety barrier, officials announced.

The bridge will be closed to motor vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists until spring 2027, according to the National Park Service.

During construction, a portion of the parkway between Big Tree Overlook at milepost 440 and the Highway 96 off-ramp at milepost 437 will also be closed. Officials said a 7.5-mile detour route will be in place, with additional travel information available online and through parkway social media channels.

“Visitor safety is our top priority,” Superintendent Wendy Ross said in a statement. “This project is an important step in ensuring the Double Arch Bridge continues to be a safe and welcoming place for everyone who visits the Natchez Trace Parkway.”

The project will replace a temporary barrier with a permanent structure designed to be more durable, effective and visually appealing. Crews will also perform preventative maintenance on the bridge, including repainting.

Officials advised bicyclists planning long-distance rides to park at the Highway 96 off-ramp and travel south of milepost 437. For shorter rides, cyclists can park at milepost 442 and ride to Big Tree Overlook and back.

Completed in 1994, the 1,572-foot Double Arch Bridge spans Birdsong Hollow at a height of about 155 feet. It was the first segmentally constructed concrete arch bridge in the United States and received the 1995 Presidential Award for Design Excellence. The structure is also considered eligible for listing on the National Register of Historic Places due to its engineering and design.

NATCHEZ — A documentary chronicling a pivotal chapter of the Civil Rights Movement in Natchez has found a permanent home at Margaret Walker Center at Jackson State University, where it is now preserved and available for free public viewing online.

The Parchman Ordeal: The Untold Story was recently added to the Center’s archives through a donation from Natchez filmmakers Robert Morgan and Darrell S. White, who co-produced the film with director G. Mark LaFrancis. LaFrancis died in June 2024 after a long battle with cancer.

The documentary, which premiered in October 2015 in Natchez, tells the story of African Americans arrested in 1965 for attempting to march for civil rights. About 150 individuals were jailed at the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman, where they endured abuse during their imprisonment.

Officials with the Margaret Walker Center said the film adds important depth to its existing civil rights archives.

“Though we have an extensive collection of civil rights interviews in our archive, this documentary sheds light on an important moment in the struggle and brings the stories of Parchman’s brave survivors to the forefront,” said Alissa Rae Funderburk, an oral historian at the Center.

Morgan said he is grateful the film will be preserved and shared with a broader audience.

“We thank the Margaret Walker Center at Jackson State University for preserving the documentary and making it accessible,” he said. “Honoring the roughly 150 young men and women arrested for parading without a permit during the civil rights era inspires future generations to boldly stand up against unconstitutional injustice.”

White said the filmmakers aimed to document the sacrifices made by those involved.

“The filmmakers’ mission was to accurately document the sacrifices made by those who took a stand on behalf of others, and the price they paid for their efforts,” he said.

Local tourism officials also praised the effort. Lynsey Gilbert, interim director of Visit Natchez, said the documentary highlights both the struggle and triumph of Natchez residents during the Civil Rights Movement and will now reach a wider audience.

The film earned recognition in 2017 as the Most Transformative Film at the Crossroads Film Festival and previously aired on Mississippi Public Broadcasting. It also served as the basis for a 2018 book detailing the events.

“The Parchman Ordeal: The Untold Story” is now available for free viewing on the Margaret Walker Center’s YouTube channel.
https://darkhorsepressnow.com/news/2026-.summary: NATCHEZ — A documentary chronicling a pivotal chapter of the Civil Rights Movement in Natchez has found a permanent home at Margaret Walker Center at Jackson State University, where it is now preserved and available for free public viewing online.

CLAIBORNE COUNTY – Two people were arrested after a reported drive-by shooting late at night on Elmwood Street in the Sugar Hill area, according to the Claiborne County Sheriff’s Office.

Authorities said deputies responded around 11:19 p.m. to a report of shots fired. A caller reported hearing multiple gunshots and seeing a black vehicle with chrome wheels leaving the area at a high rate of speed.

Deputies and the sheriff responded immediately and, while canvassing the area, spotted a black vehicle matching the description traveling from Highway 547. A traffic stop was initiated, and the occupants were detained without incident, the sheriff’s office said.

During the stop, the driver told deputies a firearm was on the back seat of the vehicle and gave consent to search it, according to investigators. Deputies said they recovered a firearm and other evidence from the vehicle.

Further investigation found the shell casings and bullets recovered from the vehicle were consistent with evidence found at the original scene, authorities said. Deputies also collected four .223 shell casings from the scene.

Investigators said both suspects admitted involvement in the shooting, which stemmed from an ongoing dispute with a person living at 1013 Elmwood St.

The sheriff’s office identified those arrested as Javeion Perkins, born April 18, 2006, of Vicksburg, and Arkeem Banks, born Nov. 4, 2007, also of Vicksburg.

Both made initial appearances before Judge Flowers, who set bond at $50,000 each.

Sheriff Edward L. Goods Sr. thanked the deputies for their quick response and arrest of the suspects.

Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced the recent sentencing of Todd Bryan Higgins, 52, known as the “Fondren Firebug,” on a trespassing conviction in Capitol Complex Improvement District Court.

According to the attorney general’s office, Higgins was sentenced April 8, 2026, by CCID Court Judge James Holland to six months in the custody of the Hinds County Detention Center, with five months to serve followed by one month of probation.

The case was investigated by Capitol Police and prosecuted by the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office.

The court also took note of Higgins’ prior interactions with law enforcement dating back to 2020, including indictments for third-degree arson and grand larceny, according to the attorney general’s office.

In announcing the sentence, Fitch also highlighted the work of the CCID Court since its creation. The attorney general’s office said it secured nearly 300 convictions in CCID Court in 2025 with a 98% success rate.

So far in 2026, prosecutors with the office have handled more than 300 initial appearances, more than 50 preliminary hearings, nearly 70 misdemeanor trials and nearly 550 traffic violations before the court, according to the attorney general’s office.

“Our office was proud to defend the law creating the CCID Court against both state and federal challenges,” Fitch said. “We were proud to work with the judges, law enforcement, prosecutors, and public defenders to stand up the court just over a year ago. And we are proud to work each day to prosecute the offenses that come before the CCID judges. We are committed to ensuring that our capital city is safe.”

JACKSON – Mississippi State Auditor Shad White announced Thursday that his office is demanding more than $7.4 million from private prison company Management & Training Corporation, saying the company failed to provide the staffing required under its contracts with the state.

According to the Mississippi Office of the State Auditor, the civil demands have also been referred to the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office for enforcement in court.

White said the auditor’s office began investigating MTC after allegations surfaced that the company was not providing the prison staff required by its contracts with the state. Investigators found that MTC failed to provide the minimum mandatory staffing levels intended to help ensure the safety of inmates and prison employees, but billed the state as though those requirements had been met, the auditor’s office said.

The auditor’s office issued three separate demands: $462,299.32 tied to staffing credits invoiced to the Mississippi Department of Corrections for the East Mississippi Correctional Facility, $959,240.06 for the Marshall County Correctional Facility and $6,002,027.92 for the Wilkinson County Correctional Facility.

“This is one of the largest civil demands made in the history of the Auditor’s Office,” White said. “We’re now turning this case over to the AG’s Office for enforcement to ensure accountability for taxpayers, and I hope they will litigate the case immediately.”

White also said his office will pursue repayment regardless of the size or influence of the company involved.

“I don’t care how big of an out-of-state company you are or how many campaign donations you make to the other politicians, if you owe taxpayers money because you failed to live up to a contract with government, we will demand you pay it back,” White said. “No free rides on the backs of taxpayers.”

The case has been referred to the attorney general’s office for possible court action.

After further investigation, officers arrested 28-year-old Kiantae J. Fair of Tupelo on April 9 and charged him with one count of cyberstalking, according to police.

On April 10, Tupelo Municipal Court Judge Weir ordered Fair held on a $4,000 bond.

Police said the case will be presented to the Lee County grand jury.

DUNDEE — A man has been arrested in connection with a shooting that occurred during a trail ride event in Dundee last month, authorities said.

Malik Javonta Vardaman, 27, of Robinsonville, was taken into custody April 11 by the Tunica County Sheriff’s Office.

The arrest stems from a March 28 shooting at a trail ride hosted on Dubbs Road by Muddy River Delta Farm.

Investigators said warrants were issued April 6 by a circuit court judge charging Vardaman with aggravated assault and discharging a firearm.

Authorities have not released additional details about the circumstances of the shooting or any victims.

The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information is urged to contact the Tunica County Sheriff’s Office at 662-363-1411 or Crime Stoppers at 662-910-0400. Officials said tips leading to an arrest could be eligible for a reward of up to $1,000.

COLUMBIA — Two people wanted on kidnapping charges out of Maryland have been arrested in Marion County, and an infant reported missing has been found safe, authorities said.

Celso Galvez Morales was taken into custody April 11 after officers with the Columbia Police Department conducted a traffic stop for speeding during proactive patrol.

During the stop, officers discovered Morales was a fugitive wanted in Maryland on kidnapping charges. A 4-month-old child in the vehicle was safely recovered and turned over to the Mississippi Department of Child Protective Services.

As the investigation continued, officers determined Morales’ girlfriend, Laura Ignacio Martinez, was also wanted in Maryland on kidnapping charges.

Police located and arrested Martinez the following day, April 12, without incident.

Both suspects are being held pending extradition to Maryland.

Authorities confirmed the juvenile connected to the case has been found safe following coordination with the Forrest County Sheriff’s Office.

Columbia Police Chief Fortenberry praised the officers involved, citing the importance of proactive policing and attention to detail.

All individuals are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

By Pam Dankins The Clarion-Ledger

Following days of testimony, Hinds County Circuit Court Judge Adrienne Wooten declared a mistrial April 9 in the murder trial of Randall Smith, who is accused of shooting and killing his Jackson State University roommate Flynn Brown in 2022.

Smith is charged with first-degree murder in the Dec. 2, 2022, death of Brown on Jackson State’s campus. Smith, 20 at the time, was on trial for murdering Brown, 22, after an altercation began over doughnuts.

Smith of New Orleans and Brown of New Jersey were suitemates living on the seventh floor of the John W. Dixon Residence Hall on Jackson State’s campus.

A Hinds County jury deliberated for more than three hours April 9 but failed to reach a unanimous decision. A mistrial was declared by Wooten.

After court, Smith was taken back to the Hinds County jail. Prosecutors will now decide whether they want to try the case again.

Following is a recap of everything we know leading up to the judge’s ruling:

Why was a mistrial declared? The jury deliberated for roughly three hours and 30 minutes April 9 before they sent a note to Wooten stating they could not reach a verdict.

When polled by Wooten, 11 of 12 jurors stated that further deliberations would not assist them with returning a verdict. When Wooten asked if returning to court the next day would assist with arriving at a unanimous verdict, at least three jurors said they were “willing to try.”

Wooten said the court is not in a position to force a jury to arrive at a decision, but it certainly has an obligation to try to determine what direction it must go in as it relates to furthering deliberation or granting a mistrial.

“Based off of what has taken place here on tonight, the court is going to grant a mistrial,” Wooten said.

After the mistrial, jurors spoke to media outlets saying all 12 members believed Smith was guilty but disagreed if Smith was guilty of first-degree murder or a lesser charge such as second-degree murder or manslaughter.

How did Flynn Brown’s family react to mistrial? Following the ruling, Flynn Brown’s mother, Michele Hill-Brown, and Flynn’s father, Michael Brown, both spoke to reporters saying that they are not going to stop fighting for justice for her son.

“We will get justice for Flynn. … (Smith) was jealous of my son in every way: his athleticism, his personality, his friendliness, his kind heart,” Michele said. “We’re going to get justice. It’s not over.”

Brown was an only child.

“You send your kid from Jersey all the way here,” Michael said. “He gets murdered, slaughtered. And then you can’t find a jury that can just understand the questions or whatever. So, what kind of system are we living in? It’s not fair. You know when I’m going to see my son? When I’m dead, in my grave.”

Defense response to mistrial After the ruling, defense attorney Kevin Dale Camp spoke to reporters April 9, saying they had hoped to get an acquittal on the case but would “T-up and do it again.” Camp also shared Smith was “disappointed” by the ruling.

“This is hard on him and his family a lot, and I think they want some closure,” Camp said. “That didn’t happen. We’ll have to figure it out a different way.”

What did Smith say in his confession to shooting Brown? During the trial, the jury listened to a recording of Smith confessing to killing Brown, stuffing Brown’s body into a storage box and dragging it outside. Once outside, Smith dumped the body inside Brown’s Dodge Challenger.

The recording also gave insight into Smith’s version of events leading up to the murder of Brown. Smith said he was eating donuts when Brown took them, leading to a fight where Brown choked him. During the struggle, Smith recalled Brown had a gun in a drawer, retrieved it and fatally shot Brown.

Smith also admitted to changing clothes and cleaning the bloody scene with bleach. Smith maintained the killing was in self-defense.

What did state, defense say to jurors in closing? Hinds County Assistant District Attorney Briana Keeler urged jurors to focus on the evidence and reject what she outlined as a web of lies spun by Smith.

Keeler said Smith lied about the incident, tried to dispose of the body and cleaned the crime scene with bleach instead of calling 911.

“Bleach is not the smell of fear,” Keeler said. “Bleach is not the smell of panic. Bleach is certainly not the smell of self-defense. That’s the smell of someone trying to erase what happened, someone trying to cover up what they did.”

The defense argued Smith removed Brown’s body and cleaned the room, believing it was the right action at the time.

“All the information that has been brought, points to one thing: that it was self-defense. (Prosecutors) have not shown that he did anything that would have negated that,” Camp said.

Pam Dankins is the breaking news reporter for the Clarion Ledger. Have a tip? Email her at [email protected] .

NATCHEZ — The City of Natchez unveiled a historical marker Wednesday honoring Prince Abdul Rahman Ibrahima on Silver Street, near the site where he arrived as an enslaved man in 1788 and later departed as a free man in 1828.

Shabilla Adams, left, and Beverly Adams are direct descendants of Prince Abdul Rahman Ibrahima. They are pictured at the new marker on Silver Street. Photo by Roscoe Barnes III

City officials said the marker commemorates Ibrahima’s journey from enslavement to freedom and highlights his connection to Natchez’s history. The marker stands near the riverfront location where he and his wife, Isabella, left Natchez on April 8, 1828.

Shelia Byrd, deputy director of the Programs and Communication Division at the Mississippi Department of Archives and History and a former Associated Press reporter, spoke during the ceremony. Byrd said the marker reflects Natchez’s willingness to acknowledge the full scope of its history, including difficult chapters tied to slavery.

Ibrahima was a Muslim prince from Timbo in the Futa Jallon region of present-day Guinea in West Africa. According to the city, he was captured in battle in 1788, sold to slave traders and endured 40 years of enslavement on Thomas Foster’s plantation near Natchez before gaining his freedom.

Mayor Dan Gibson said the city has a responsibility to tell the full story of those who helped build Natchez. He said Ibrahima’s story represents not only one man’s life but also the broader history of enslaved people whose labor shaped the community.

The Silver Street marker is the second historical marker in the Natchez-Adams County area honoring Ibrahima. The first was unveiled in October 2025 on Highway 61 North near Historic Jefferson College and focuses on his 1807 meeting with Dr. John Coates Cox. City officials said the new marker emphasizes his West African roots and the site of his departure to freedom.
